title: Which Roti Wins on Protein, Fibre, Iron and Calcium? Nutritionist's Answer
excerpt: Nutritionist Kiran Kukreja's comparison finds ragi leads on calcium, amaranth on protein and bajra on magnesium — but her real advice is to rotate grains, not abandon wheat.
body:
• A nutritionist's viral comparison of six alternative rotis finds wheat isn't the nutrient leader: ragi leads on calcium, amaranth on protein, and bajra on magnesium and iron.
  • Ahmedabad-based nutritionist Kiran Kukreja recommends rotating jowar, ragi, bajra, jau, makki and amaranth instead of eating wheat roti every day.
  • Her bottom line: wheat roti doesn't need to go — variety does the work. But each grain has caveats, from bajra's thyroid caution to ragi's kidney caution.
  • Independent nutrition data backs the broad strokes: ragi carries about 344 mg of calcium per 100 g — roughly ten times wheat — while amaranth's protein is complete with all nine essential amino acids.

If roti shows up at every meal in your house, which one is actually doing the most for you? The wheat roti on your plate may not be the answer. In a September 8, 2026 post that went viral, Ahmedabad-based nutritionist Kiran Kukreja compared six alternatives — jau (barley), jowar (sorghum), bajra (pearl millet), ragi (finger millet), makki (maize) and amaranth (rajgira) — and found that each beats wheat on at least one of the big five nutrients: protein, fibre, iron, calcium and magnesium.

What the comparison actually says

Kukreja's post, reported by Hindustan Times, is qualitative rather than a lab table — it describes each grain's strengths rather than per-roti numbers. The standouts: amaranth is the only grain she describes as "high in protein," alongside iron and calcium, and it is naturally gluten-free; ragi is "high in calcium, iron and fibre," supporting bone health and diabetes management; bajra is "rich in magnesium, iron and fibre," helping with anaemia, cholesterol and constipation; makki is "rich in vitamin A, fibre and magnesium," warming and good for eye health; jowar is gluten-free, good for diabetes, increases satiety and boosts metabolism; and barley has a low glycemic index, good for diabetes and weight loss.

Independent nutrition data backs the broad strokes. Per 100 g of grain, ragi carries roughly 344 mg of calcium — the highest of any cereal, about ten times whole wheat's 30–40 mg, per ICMR/ICAR data published in Springer Planta. Amaranth runs about 13–14 g of protein per 100 g, the only one of the six with a complete amino-acid profile, plus around 7.6 mg of iron and 248 mg of magnesium. Bajra and jowar sit at 10–12 g of protein per 100 g, comparable to or above wheat's roughly 11.8 g — wheat's real weakness is minerals, not protein.

The catch: not every grain suits everybody

Kukreja is careful with caveats. Barley contains gluten, so it is out for celiac disease. Jowar can feel heavy for severe IBS or sensitive digestion. Bajra contains goitrogens and should be used cautiously with thyroid issues — and it is a winter grain in her framework, not a peak-summer one. Ragi is high in phosphorus, a caution for kidney issues, and can be hard on very weak digestion. Makki, despite the fibre, is not her pick for people with diabetes. Amaranth is the most forgiving — avoid only in rare allergy cases.

The real takeaway: rotate, don't ban

The most useful line in the post isn't about any single grain. "And no, you don't need to completely stop eating wheat roti," Kukreja wrote. "The key is variety — rotate your grains and choose what suits your body best."

"If roti is a daily part of your meals, don't just stick to the same atta every day... These grains can add more fibre, protein, iron, calcium, magnesium and other micronutrients to your diet, while also keeping your meals more diverse and filling."

— Kiran Kukreja, nutritionist, via Hindustan Times

Diaspora angle

For NRIs, this is an easy upgrade: every one of these flours — ragi, jowar, bajra, makki, rajgira atta — is stocked in Indian grocery stores across the US and Canada, usually at prices close to wheat atta. Rotating grains also matches what many diaspora kitchens already do seasonally, like makki di roti in winter.

A note of caution

Hindustan Times notes its report is based on user-generated social-media content that it has not independently verified, and the article is informational only — not medical advice. Anyone managing diabetes, kidney disease, thyroid conditions or celiac disease should check with a doctor or dietitian before changing staple grains.
